claim: Twenty healthy adults (10 males and 10 females, mean age 24 years) participated in the study.
source: Twenty healthy adults with normal or corrected vision (10 males and 10 females, mean age 24 years) participated in the study.
evidence: Direct statement in the methods section describing participant demographics.

claim: The study was approved by the regional ethics committee (CPP Ile de France VII, Hôpital de Bicêtre, No. 15–007).
source: The study was approved by the regional ethics committee (CPP Ile de France VII, Hôpital de Bicêtre, No. 15–007) and all participants gave written informed consent.
evidence: Direct statement about ethical approval.

claim: Functional images were acquired on a SIEMENS MAGNETOM 7T scanner.
source: Functional images were acquired on a SIEMENS MAGNETOM 7T scanner with head gradient insert (Gmax 80mT/m and slew rate 333 T/m/s) and adapted 32-channel head coil (Nova Medical, Wilmington, MA, USA)
evidence: Direct statement about the MRI scanner used.

claim: Response accuracies for comparison of match stimuli were 86% for the number task and 85% for the average size task.
source: Response accuracies for comparison of match stimuli were overall high and not significantly different across tasks (86% for the number task and 85% for the average size task, t(19) = 0.46, p = 0.65)
evidence: Direct statement of behavioral performance data with statistical test.

claim: Task difficulty was successfully matched across the number and size tasks.
source: Response accuracies for comparison of match stimuli were overall high and not significantly different across tasks (86% for the number task and 85% for the average size task, t(19) = 0.46, p = 0.65), suggesting that subjects attended to the correct stimulus dimension and the difficulty was on average successfully matched across tasks (Figure 2A).
evidence: Inference from non-significant difference in accuracy between tasks.

claim: The direct contrast of sample stimulus-related activity during the number versus the size task revealed no area with significantly stronger activation for either of the two tasks.
source: The direct contrast of sample stimulus-related activity during the number versus the size task revealed no area with significantly stronger activation for either of the two, despite the uncorrected significance threshold (Figure 2D).
evidence: Direct statement about univariate fMRI contrast results, with reference to Figure 2D.

claim: Sample numerosity could be decoded significantly above chance in all ROIs during both the number and size tasks.
source: Overall, the presented sample numerosity could be decoded significantly above chance in all the ROIs and during both the number and size task, however with important differences.
evidence: Direct statement about multivariate classification results.

claim: When attending to numerosity, classification accuracy gradually increased across the dorsal stream and was highest in parietal areas.
source: When explicitly attending to numerosity, the classification accuracy gradually increased across the dorsal stream (starting to be enhanced from intermediate areas, specifically from V3AB on), and was highest in parietal areas.
evidence: Direct statement about the pattern of classification accuracy across brain regions during the number task.

claim: During the size task, classification accuracies for numerosity were reduced in intermediate and higher regions but remained almost unchanged in early visual areas.
source: During the size task, when attention was not explicitly directed towards the numerical aspect of the stimuli, the different numerosities were still decodable, however the classification accuracies were reduced in intermediate and higher regions, while they remained almost unchanged in early visual areas (specifically in V1, V2 and V3).
evidence: Direct statement about classification accuracy patterns during the size task.

claim: The task-driven modulation of decoding accuracies across the three major ROIs is confirmed by a significant interaction between ROI and task (F(1.69,32.11) = 9.81, p = 0.0008).
source: The task-driven modulation of decoding accuracies across the three major ROIs is confirmed by a significant interaction between ROI and task (F(1.69,32.11) = 9.81, p = 0.0008).
evidence: Direct statement of statistical test result.

claim: Beta weights for number were generally positive and progressively explained the activity patterns better when proceeding from lower to higher-level regions when task relevant.
source: Beta weights for the effect of number independent of the other dimensions (black triangles) were generally positive and progressively explained the activity patterns better when proceeding from lower to higher-level regions when task relevant.
evidence: Direct statement about RSA regression results for numerosity.

claim: Beta weights for the non-numerical dimensions were pronounced predominantly in the earlier visual areas and appeared to be not clearly affected by task.
source: Beta weights for the non-numerical dimensions (other shapes in Figure 5) were pronounced predominantly in the earlier visual areas and, importantly, they appeared to be not clearly affected by task.
evidence: Direct statement about RSA regression results for non-numerical dimensions, with reference to Figure 5.

claim: The triple interaction between ROI, task and dimension was significant for the three large regions (F(2.86,54.43) = 4.73, p = 0.006) and for the individual regions (F(4.52,85.95) = 3.34, p = 0.01).
source: The significant triple interaction between ROI, task and dimension confirmed that the beta weights estimated for the different dimensions were differently affected by task across ROIs (for the three large regions: F(4.23, 80.40) = 3.32, p = 0.01; for the individual regions: F(6.18,117.38) = 3.06, p = 0.007).
evidence: Direct statement of statistical test result.

claim: Beta values for number showed a significant interaction between ROI and task when comparing the three large subdivisions across the visual stream (F(1.35,25.62) = 5.97, p = 0.015).
source: Beta values for number were the only ones showing a significant interaction between ROI and task, when comparing the three large subdivisions across the visual stream (F(1.35,25.62) = 5.97, p = 0.015).
evidence: Direct statement of statistical test result.

claim: During the number task, betas for number were higher in intermediate and higher-level areas with respect to early visual areas.
source: During the number task, betas for number were higher in intermediate and higher-level areas with respect to early visual areas (although only the former comparison was significant, p = 0.04, Cohen's d = 0.70).
evidence: Direct statement about comparison of beta weights across regions.

claim: During the size task, betas for number were significantly lower than during the number task in early, intermediate, and higher areas.
source: During the size task the betas for number were significantly lower (significant difference across tasks in early: p = 0.007, Cohen's d = 0.78; intermediate: p = 0.000001, Cohen's d = 1.96; higher areas: p = 0.00001, Cohen's d = 1.43) and not different across regions.
evidence: Direct statement of statistical comparisons.

claim: The increase in beta weights for number across the dorsal visual stream was significant during the number task only (F(1,5) = 14.23, p = 0.01, R2 = 0.74).
source: Although post-hoc tests did not identify significant differences across ROIs, linear regression showed that the increase in beta weights for number across the dorsal visual stream was significant during the number task only (F(1,5) = 14.23, p = 0.01, R2 = 0.74), while during the size task betas for number were much more homogenous across ROIs (F(1,5)=2.37, p = 0.18, R2 = 0.32).
evidence: Direct statement of linear regression results.

claim: Beta weights estimated for the non-numerical dimensions were not modulated by task for any of the dimensions.
source: Different from number, beta weights estimated for the non-numerical dimensions were not modulated by task (no significant interaction between ROIs and task, no significant main effect of task) for any of the dimensions.
evidence: Direct statement about lack of task effects on non-numerical dimensions.

claim: Total field area best explained activity patterns in early visual areas, and its contribution was reduced when proceeding through intermediate to higher-level areas.
source: Independent of the task, total field area best explained activity patterns in early visual areas, while its contribution was reduced when proceeding through intermediate to higher-level areas (significant main effect of ROIs: F(1.23, 23.29)=35.24, p = 0.000002; significant differences in beta weights between primary and intermediate or higher-level ROIs: p = 0.000155, Cohen's d = 1.24, p = 0.000008, Cohen's d = 1.80, respectively).
evidence: Direct statement about RSA results for total field area with statistical tests.

claim: Total surface area most strongly modulated pattern dissimilarity in early visual areas.
source: Total surface area also most strongly modulated pattern dissimilarity in early visual areas. The significant main effect of ROI (F(1.45,27.63) = 16.61, p = 0.000078) and the following post-hoc tests showed that beta values for this dimension in the early visual areas were significantly higher than those estimated for the intermediate (p = 0.000475, Cohen's d = 0.76) and higher-level (p = 0.000943, Cohen's d = 1.30) ROIs, independent of the task.
evidence: Direct statement about RSA results for total surface area with statistical tests.

claim: Effects due to average item size could not be detected in any of the ROIs tested.
source: Surprisingly, effects due to average item size could not be detected in any of the ROIs tested.
evidence: Direct statement about lack of effects for average item size.

claim: Intraparietal cortex is thought to provide a crucial substrate for the ability to base decisions on estimates of number.
source: Humans and other animals base important decisions on estimates of number, and intraparietal cortex is thought to provide a crucial substrate of this ability.
evidence: Statement in the abstract reflecting established scientific understanding.

claim: Numerosity explained a significant amount of variance in activation patterns along the dorsal visual stream, above and beyond non-numerical dimensions.
source: Along the dorsal visual stream, numerosity explained a significant amount of variance in activation patterns, above and beyond non-numerical dimensions.
evidence: Direct statement of main finding in the abstract.

claim: Numerosity representation was selectively amplified and progressively enhanced across the hierarchy when task relevant.
source: Its representation was selectively amplified and progressively enhanced across the hierarchy when task relevant.
evidence: Direct statement of main finding in the abstract.

claim: The results reveal a sensory extraction mechanism yielding information on numerosity separable from other dimensions already at early visual stages.
source: Our results reveal a sensory extraction mechanism yielding information on numerosity separable from other dimensions already at early visual stages and suggest that later regions along the dorsal stream are most important for explicit manipulation of numerical quantity.
evidence: Direct statement of interpretation of results in the abstract.

claim: Later regions along the dorsal stream are most important for explicit manipulation of numerical quantity.
source: Our results reveal a sensory extraction mechanism yielding information on numerosity separable from other dimensions already at early visual stages and suggest that later regions along the dorsal stream are most important for explicit manipulation of numerical quantity.
evidence: Direct statement of interpretation of results in the abstract.

claim: The 'number sense' is a phylogenetically ancient competence that enables humans and other animals to assess and mentally manipulate the approximate number of objects in sets.
source: This is a phylogenetically ancient competence that enables humans and other animals to assess and mentally manipulate the approximate number of objects in sets.
evidence: Statement in the introduction reflecting established theory.

claim: In humans, the precision of the number sense sharpens with age and with the acquisition of formal mathematical education (Piazza et al., 2013).
source: In humans the precision of the number sense (or 'numerical acuity', typically measured by visual number discrimination) sharpens with age and with the acquisition of formal mathematical education (Piazza et al., 2013)
evidence: Statement supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Numerical acuity correlates with arithmetical skills throughout the life-span (Halberda et al., 2008; Libertus et al., 2011; Libertus et al., 2013; Chen and Li, 2014; Anobile et al., 2016a; Anobile et al., 2018).
source: and correlates with arithmetical skills throughout the life-span (Halberda et al., 2008; Libertus et al., 2011; Libertus et al., 2013; Chen and Li, 2014; Anobile et al., 2016a; Anobile et al., 2018).
evidence: Statement supported by multiple citations.

claim: Deviations from the typical developmental trend of numerical acuity can be a symptom of developmental dyscalculia (Piazza et al., 2010).
source: Deviations from the typical developmental trend of numerical acuity can be a symptom of developmental dyscalculia (Piazza et al., 2010), a neurodevelopmental disorder that causes specific mathematical learning difficulties.
evidence: Statement supported by citation.

claim: The neural substrate subtending the sense of numerical quantity is thought to be shared across species.
source: The neural substrate subtending this sense of numerical quantity is thought to be shared across species and has been linked to a network of areas in the frontal and parietal cortices sensitive to changes in numerosity since very early in life (Izard et al., 2008; Hyde and Spelke, 2011; see for reviews: Cantlon, 2012; de Hevia et al., 2017).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Electrophysiological recordings in monkeys identified single neurons tuned to specific numerosities of visual arrays (Nieder et al., 2002; Nieder and Miller, 2004; Roitman et al., 2007; Nieder, 2016).
source: In these areas electrophysiological recordings in monkeys identified single neurons tuned to specific numerosities of visual arrays (Nieder et al., 2002; Nieder and Miller, 2004; Roitman et al., 2007; Nieder, 2016)
evidence: Statement supported by citations to electrophysiology studies.

claim: fMRI studies in humans found activation in frontal and parietal areas to be modulated during quantity perception as well as during calculation (Arsalidou and Taylor, 2011; Eger, 2016; Piazza and Eger, 2016).
source: and fMRI studies in humans found activation in these areas to be modulated during quantity perception as well as during calculation (for reviews see: Arsalidou and Taylor, 2011; Eger, 2016; Piazza and Eger, 2016).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to review articles.

claim: fMRI adaptation and multivariate pattern analysis methods provide higher sensitivity to finer-scale activity differences (Kourtzi and Grill-Spector, 2005; Norman et al., 2006; Tong and Pratte, 2012).
source: While the first imaging studies in humans were limited by the low spatial resolution and univariate subtraction-based analyses, fMRI adaptation and multivariate pattern analysis methods provide higher sensitivity to finer-scale activity differences (Kourtzi and Grill-Spector, 2005; Norman et al., 2006; Tong and Pratte, 2012).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to methodological papers.

claim: Population-receptive field mapping methods identified individual locations tuned to specific numerosities arranged in spatially organized maps in the parietal cortex (Harvey et al., 2013).
source: Moreover, population-receptive field mapping (pRF) methods identified individual locations tuned to specific numerosities arranged in spatially organized maps in the parietal cortex (Harvey et al., 2013).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to previous research.

claim: It is possible to decode the number of items from fMRI activity patterns in early visual areas (Bulthé et al., 2014; Eger et al., 2015; Bulthé et al., 2015; DeWind et al., 2019).
source: While these earlier findings mostly pointed at the key role of parietal and frontal areas in numerical representation, some recent studies found that it is possible to decode the number of items seen by the subjects from the fMRI activity patterns in early visual areas (Bulthé et al., 2014; Eger et al., 2015; Bulthé et al., 2015; DeWind et al., 2019, but see Castaldi et al., 2016).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to recent studies.

claim: Spatially organized numerosity maps were recently claimed to extend to the occipital cortex (Harvey and Dumoulin, 2017a).
source: Moreover, spatially organized numerosity maps were recently claimed to extend to the occipital cortex (Harvey and Dumoulin, 2017a)
evidence: Statement supported by citation.

claim: Early ERP components compatible with generators in early visual areas responded to variations in the numerosity of visual arrays (Park et al., 2015; Fornaciai et al., 2017; Fornaciai and Park, 2017).
source: and early ERP components compatible with generators in early visual areas responded to variations in the numerosity of visual arrays (Park et al., 2015; Fornaciai et al., 2017; Fornaciai and Park, 2017).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to ERP studies.

claim: Several properties characterizing numerosity perception, such as being ratio-dependent (Weber's law) and being susceptible to adaptation, led some authors to suggest that number is a 'primary' visual property (Burr and Ross, 2008; Ross, 2010; Anobile et al., 2016b).
source: Several properties characterizing numerosity perception, such as being ratio-dependent (Weber's law) and being susceptible to adaptation, led some authors to suggest that number is a 'primary' visual property of the image that is directly perceived through specialized and dedicated mechanisms (Burr and Ross, 2008; Ross, 2010; Anobile et al., 2016b).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to theoretical papers.

claim: It remains debated whether the available evidence supports a sensory extraction mechanism directly sensitive to numerosity.
source: For this reason, in spite of a large body of behavioral and neuroscientific work on this topic, it still remains debated whether the available evidence supports a sensory extraction mechanism directly sensitive to numerosity.
evidence: Statement about ongoing scientific debate.

claim: Some have argued that numerosity might be judged indirectly by weighing a combination of other, non-numerical, quantitative features of the stimuli (Gebuis and Reynvoet, 2012; Gebuis et al., 2014; Leibovich et al., 2016a).
source: Some have argued instead that numerosity might be judged indirectly by weighing a combination of other, non-numerical, quantitative features of the stimuli (Gebuis and Reynvoet, 2012; Gebuis et al., 2014; Leibovich et al., 2016a).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to alternative theoretical views.

claim: The discrimination of numerosity and of item density follow different psychophysical laws (Anobile et al., 2016b).
source: While this possibility is interesting, several behavioral findings argue against it: (1) the discrimination of numerosity and of one often correlated non-numerical feature (item density) follow different psychophysical laws (Anobile et al., 2016b)
evidence: Statement supported by citation to behavioral study.

claim: For relatively small numbers of not too densely spaced items, perceptual thresholds for numerosity discrimination are typically much smaller than the ones predicted from the thresholds for density and field area together (Cicchini et al., 2016).
source: and (2) at least for relatively small numbers of not too densely spaced items, perceptual thresholds for numerosity discrimination are typically much smaller than the ones predicted from the thresholds for density and field area together (Cicchini et al., 2016), making it unlikely that estimates of numerosity are based on the latter.
evidence: Statement supported by citation to behavioral study.

claim: Attention to basic visual features either increases the gain or sharpens responses of neuronal populations preferentially responsive to these features in different visual areas (Treue and Martínez Trujillo, 1999; McAdams and Maunsell, 2000; Reynolds et al., 2000; Martinez-Trujillo and Treue, 2004; David et al., 2008).
source: Neurophysiological studies have shown that attention to basic visual features either increases the gain or sharpens responses of neuronal populations preferentially responsive to these features in different visual areas (e.g. Treue and Martínez Trujillo, 1999; McAdams and Maunsell, 2000; Reynolds et al., 2000; Martinez-Trujillo and Treue, 2004; David et al., 2008), see also: Carrasco (2011) for a review).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to neurophysiology studies.

claim: fMRI decoding studies have found that directing attention to one feature dimension improves the read-out of these features from brain activity in early sensory regions (Kamitani and Tong, 2005; Kamitani and Tong, 2006; Serences and Boynton, 2007; Jehee et al., 2011).
source: Correspondingly, fMRI decoding studies have found that directing attention to one feature dimension such as orientation, motion direction or color or to particular values within one given dimension improves the read-out of these features from brain activity in early sensory regions (Kamitani and Tong, 2005; Kamitani and Tong, 2006; Serences and Boynton, 2007; Jehee et al., 2011) but in some cases also in higher-level areas (Liu et al., 2011; Ester et al., 2016).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to fMRI studies.

claim: Higher-level fronto-parietal areas such as the lateral intraparietal area (LIP) implement spatial 'priority maps' (Itti and Koch, 2001; Thompson and Bichot, 2005; Gottlieb, 2007; Sapountzis et al., 2018).
source: According to one influential account, higher-level fronto-parietal areas such as the lateral intraparietal area (LIP) implement spatial 'priority maps' in which the level of activity at individual locations depends jointly on the different features of objects at these locations as well as on top-down factors such as their task relevance, associated reward, etc (Itti and Koch, 2001; Thompson and Bichot, 2005; Gottlieb, 2007; Sapountzis et al., 2018).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to theoretical and empirical papers.

claim: LIP neurons have been found to represent higher-level factors such as learned category membership and other non-spatial information (Freedman and Assad, 2009).
source: Independent of spatial priority, LIP neurons have also been found to represent higher-level factors such as learned category membership and other non-spatial information (Freedman and Assad, 2009)
evidence: Statement supported by citation.

claim: LIP neurons flexibly switch between encoding of different visual features, such as color or motion, depending on the task (Toth and Assad, 2002; Ibos and Freedman, 2014).
source: and to flexibly switch between encoding of different visual features, such as color or motion, depending on the task (Toth and Assad, 2002; Ibos and Freedman, 2014).
evidence: Statement supported by citations.

claim: The existence of individual neurons tuned to different numbers of items in intraparietal cortex is well established (Nieder and Miller, 2004; Roitman et al., 2007).
source: While the existence of individual neurons tuned to different numbers of items in intraparietal cortex is well established (Nieder and Miller, 2004; Roitman et al., 2007)
evidence: Statement supported by citations to electrophysiology studies.

claim: Neurons in the ventral intraparietal (VIP) cortex in macaque monkeys encoded numerosity to the same extent, regardless of whether the task required attending to number or color (Viswanathan and Nieder, 2015).
source: the only electrophysiological study that recorded from neurons in the ventral intraparietal (VIP) cortex in macaque monkeys under changing task conditions (Viswanathan and Nieder, 2015) found that neurons encoded numerosity to the same extent, regardless of whether the task required to attend to the number or the color of the items.
evidence: Statement supported by citation to electrophysiology study.

claim: The human IPS 1–5 is usually considered to be the equivalent of the macaque LIP/VIP complex (Kastner et al., 2017).
source: Given that the human IPS 1–5 investigated in the current work is usually considered to be the equivalent of the macaque LIP/VIP complex (Kastner et al., 2017)
evidence: Statement supported by citation.

claim: The precision of numerical representation is predictive of formal arithmetic and gets refined with development and mathematical learning (Halberda and Feigenson, 2008; Nys et al., 2013; Piazza, 2010; Piazza et al., 2010; Piazza et al., 2013).
source: While earlier behavioral research suggested that the precision of numerical representation is predictive of formal arithmetic and gets refined with development and mathematical learning (Halberda and Feigenson, 2008; Nys et al., 2013; Piazza, 2010; Piazza et al., 2010; Piazza et al., 2013)
evidence: Statement supported by citations to behavioral studies.

claim: What might be changing with development and mathematical competence could be the ability to focus on numerical information while filtering out non-numerical dimensions during a numerical comparison task (Castaldi et al., 2018; Piazza et al., 2018; Starr et al., 2017; Wilkey et al., 2018).
source: other recent evidence has led to a slightly different view: what might be changing with development and mathematical competence could be the ability to focus on numerical information while filtering out non-numerical dimensions during a numerical comparison task (Castaldi et al., 2018; Piazza et al., 2018; Starr et al., 2017; Wilkey et al., 2018).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to recent studies.

claim: The influence of non-numerical dimensions on numerical judgments decreases over normotypical development (Bugden and Ansari, 2016; Piazza et al., 2018; Szucs et al., 2013; Wilkey et al., 2018).
source: The influence of non-numerical dimensions on numerical judgments decreases over normotypical development and both dyscalculic children (Bugden and Ansari, 2016; Piazza et al., 2018; Szucs et al., 2013; Wilkey et al., 2018) and adults (Castaldi et al., 2018) seem to be disproportionately affected by non-numerical dimensions during numerical comparison tasks.
evidence: Statement supported by citations to developmental studies.

claim: Dyscalculic children and adults seem to be disproportionately affected by non-numerical dimensions during numerical comparison tasks (Bugden and Ansari, 2016; Piazza et al., 2018; Szucs et al., 2013; Wilkey et al., 2018; Castaldi et al., 2018).
source: The influence of non-numerical dimensions on numerical judgments decreases over normotypical development and both dyscalculic children (Bugden and Ansari, 2016; Piazza et al., 2018; Szucs et al., 2013; Wilkey et al., 2018) and adults (Castaldi et al., 2018) seem to be disproportionately affected by non-numerical dimensions during numerical comparison tasks.
evidence: Statement supported by citations to studies on dyscalculia.

claim: Mechanisms for average size perception may rely on texture processing mechanisms rather than individual item identification (Im and Halberda, 2013).
source: It has been previously suggested that average item size perception, like density perception, may rely on texture processing mechanisms rather than individual item identification (Im and Halberda, 2013).
evidence: Statement supported by citation.

claim: Adaptation studies have identified recovery of fMRI signal in the medial part of the posterior collateral sulcus that was selective for texture as opposed to color or shape of 3D irregular objects (Cavina-Pratesi et al., 2010).
source: In particular, adaptation studies have identified recovery of fMRI signal in the medial part of the posterior collateral sulcus that was selective for texture as opposed to color or shape of 3D irregular objects (Cavina-Pratesi et al., 2010)
evidence: Statement supported by citation to fMRI study.

claim: The parahippocampal place area (PPA) showed equal release from adaptation for object ensemble and surface textures, suggesting that ensembles and textures are processed similarly (Cant and Xu, 2012).
source: and the parahippocampal place area (PPA) showed equal release from adaptation for object ensemble and surface textures, suggesting that ensembles and textures are processed similarly (Cant and Xu, 2012).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to fMRI study.

claim: Arrays of six, ten or seventeen dots were created with three average item areas (0.04, 0.07 and 0.12 visual degree2) and displayed within two total field areas.
source: Arrays of six, ten or seventeen dots were created with three average item areas (0.04, 0.07 and 0.12 visual degree2) and displayed within two total field areas, enclosed by imaginary circles of 5° (TFA 1) and 7.5° (TFA 2) diameter.
evidence: Direct statement about stimulus parameters, with reference to Figure 1A.

claim: Participants alternated between a 'number' and a 'size' task in different blocks.
source: Participants alternated between a 'number' and a 'size' task in different blocks: during the 'number' blocks they had to direct attention to the numerosity of each sample stimulus and keep it in memory for comparison with an occasionally following match stimulus, while during 'size' blocks they performed the equivalent task on the average item size of the arrays (Figure 1B).
evidence: Direct statement about experimental design, with reference to Figure 1B.

claim: The study exploited the enhanced sensitivity achieved by fMRI at ultra-high field (7 Tesla).
source: We exploited the enhanced sensitivity achieved by fMRI at ultra-high field (7 Tesla) and specific multivariate pattern analyses to simultaneously model and separate the contributions of numerical and different non-numerical quantities to fine-scale activity patterns within multiple regions defined by a probabilistic atlas based on visual topography.
evidence: Direct statement about methodological approach.

claim: Attending to different quantitative dimensions leads to equivalent overall activation of the brain regions involved in the task.
source: Altogether, these results suggest that task difficulty was successfully matched and that under these conditions attending to different quantitative dimensions leads to equivalent overall activation of the brain regions involved in the task.
evidence: Inference from univariate fMRI results.

claim: The numerical information at early visual areas was only to a minor extent modulated by task.
source: Finally, although present starting from the earliest stages of visual analysis, the numerical information at this level was only to a minor extent modulated by task and the greatest contribution to explicit manipulation of numerical quantity was found in intermediate and higher-level regions.
evidence: Summary statement of findings.

claim: The greatest contribution to explicit manipulation of numerical quantity was found in intermediate and higher-level regions.
source: Finally, although present starting from the earliest stages of visual analysis, the numerical information at this level was only to a minor extent modulated by task and the greatest contribution to explicit manipulation of numerical quantity was found in intermediate and higher-level regions.
evidence: Summary statement of findings.

claim: Early visual areas contained independent information on multiple quantitative properties of which some explained more variance than numerosity.
source: In sum, while early visual areas contained independent information on multiple quantitative properties of which some explained more variance than numerosity, all regions were modulated to some extent by numerical distance over and above what was explainable by the non-numerical dimensions.
evidence: Summary statement of RSA results.

claim: All regions were modulated to some extent by numerical distance over and above what was explainable by the non-numerical dimensions.
source: In sum, while early visual areas contained independent information on multiple quantitative properties of which some explained more variance than numerosity, all regions were modulated to some extent by numerical distance over and above what was explainable by the non-numerical dimensions.
evidence: Summary statement of RSA results.

claim: Explicitly directing attention to number enhanced the representation of numerical information selectively, without altering the representations of non-numerical quantities.
source: Moreover, importantly, explicitly directing attention to number did enhance the representation of numerical information and did so selectively, without altering the representations of non-numerical quantities.
evidence: Summary statement of attentional modulation findings.

claim: The study provides direct neuroscientific evidence for a sensory processing mechanism capable of disentangling signals related to visual numerosity from the ones related to associated non-numerical quantities from early stages of cortical processing on.
source: In conclusion, with this study using high-resolution, high-field fMRI we provide direct neuroscientific evidence for a sensory processing mechanism capable of disentangling signals related to visual numerosity from the ones related to associated non-numerical quantities from early stages of cortical processing on, which can then be independently and progressively amplified across the dorsal visual stream when numerical information is explicitly task-relevant.
evidence: Summary statement of main conclusion.

claim: Numerical information can be independently and progressively amplified across the dorsal visual stream when numerical information is explicitly task-relevant.
source: In conclusion, with this study using high-resolution, high-field fMRI we provide direct neuroscientific evidence for a sensory processing mechanism capable of disentangling signals related to visual numerosity from the ones related to associated non-numerical quantities from early stages of cortical processing on, which can then be independently and progressively amplified across the dorsal visual stream when numerical information is explicitly task-relevant.
evidence: Summary statement of main conclusion.

claim: The numerical information read out from early visual areas could reflect a location map or the process of object segmentation.
source: As one speculative interpretation, the numerical information read out from early visual areas could reflect a location map (Dehaene and Changeux, 1993), or the process of object segmentation where different individual items start to be separately represented, but this representation may not yet be in a form that is most easily read out for numerical discrimination.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of findings with citation.

claim: Higher areas may progressively transform and concentrate the initially distributed information onto individual neurons.
source: Higher areas may progressively transform and concentrate the initially distributed information onto individual neurons, which most likely constitute the base on which we operate when comparing numbers.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of findings.

claim: The behavioral precision of numerical discrimination was correlated with the decoding accuracy only in parietal cortex (Lasne et al., 2019).
source: This interpretation is in line with a recent study showing that although different numerosities could be discriminated based on the pattern of activity in early visual areas and parietal cortex, the behavioral precision of numerical discrimination was correlated with the decoding accuracy only in the latter region (Lasne et al., 2019).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to recent study.

claim: Numerosity can be mathematically defined as the product of density by field area.
source: For example, numerosity can be mathematically defined as the product of density (number of items per unit of area) by field area; or by the total surface area divided by mean item size.
evidence: Statement of mathematical relationship.

claim: Numerosity can be mathematically defined by the total surface area divided by mean item size.
source: For example, numerosity can be mathematically defined as the product of density (number of items per unit of area) by field area; or by the total surface area divided by mean item size.
evidence: Statement of mathematical relationship.

claim: If a brain area encodes numerical information in a way that is separable from associated non-numerical dimensions, tasks involving selective attention to number should enhance the information about numerosity, without affecting the level of information on associated non-numerical dimensions.
source: If a brain area encodes numerical information in a way that is separable from associated non-numerical dimensions, tasks involving selective attention to number should enhance the information about numerosity, without affecting the level of information on associated non-numerical dimensions.
evidence: Theoretical prediction stated by the authors.

claim: The presence of independent attentional amplification is a key criterion in order to identify which brain areas explicitly encode information on numerosity.
source: Thus, we propose that the presence of such independent attentional amplification is a key criterion in order to identify which brain areas explicitly encode information on numerosity.
evidence: Theoretical criterion proposed by the authors.

claim: If numerosity was not directly encoded but only indirectly inferred from percepts of non-numerical properties, attentional enhancement should not occur for signals related to numerosity.
source: Furthermore, if numerosity was not directly encoded but only indirectly inferred from percepts of non-numerical properties, attentional enhancement should not occur for signals related to numerosity, but if anything, only for other properties (e.g., density and field area) that can jointly define it.
evidence: Theoretical prediction stated by the authors.

claim: If activity patterns could be entirely accounted for by the combination of responses to multiple non-numerical dimensions of the stimuli, no information specifically related to number should be found in the patterns of activity once accounting for the other dimensions simultaneously.
source: On the contrary, if activity patterns could be entirely accounted for by the combination of responses to multiple non-numerical dimensions of the stimuli, no information specifically related to number should be found in the patterns of activity once accounting for the other (non-numerical) dimensions simultaneously.
evidence: Theoretical prediction stated by the authors.

claim: The study created a novel stimulus space to disentangle the contribution of numerical and non-numerical dimensions to brain activity patterns.
source: To test these predictions, we created a novel stimulus space to disentangle the contribution of numerical and non-numerical dimensions to brain activity patterns, and designed a task where attention is selectively directed towards either of two orthogonal quantitative dimensions of the visual array (number or item size).
evidence: Direct statement about experimental design.

claim: The study designed a task where attention is selectively directed towards either number or item size.
source: To test these predictions, we created a novel stimulus space to disentangle the contribution of numerical and non-numerical dimensions to brain activity patterns, and designed a task where attention is selectively directed towards either of two orthogonal quantitative dimensions of the visual array (number or item size).
evidence: Direct statement about experimental design.

claim: Attending to the numerosity or to the average size of the dots in the array recruited largely overlapping occipital and parietal areas.
source: At the level of overall regional activity, attending to the numerosity or to the average size of the dots in the array recruited largely overlapping occipital and parietal areas, as also previously observed for perception and comparison of different types of quantities (Pinel et al., 2004; Dormal and Pesenti, 2009; Borghesani et al., 2019); for a meta-analysis on other non-numerical representations see: Sokolowski et al., 2017).
evidence: Statement of finding with citations to previous studies.

claim: The study used specific multivariate pattern analyses to simultaneously model and separate the contributions of numerical and different non-numerical quantities to fine-scale activity patterns.
source: We exploited the enhanced sensitivity achieved by fMRI at ultra-high field (7 Tesla) and specific multivariate pattern analyses to simultaneously model and separate the contributions of numerical and different non-numerical quantities to fine-scale activity patterns within multiple regions defined by a probabilistic atlas based on visual topography.
evidence: Direct statement about analytical approach.

claim: Multiple regions were defined by a probabilistic atlas based on visual topography (Wang et al., 2015).
source: We exploited the enhanced sensitivity achieved by fMRI at ultra-high field (7 Tesla) and specific multivariate pattern analyses to simultaneously model and separate the contributions of numerical and different non-numerical quantities to fine-scale activity patterns within multiple regions defined by a probabilistic atlas based on visual topography.
evidence: Direct statement about ROI definition with citation.

claim: The interaction between ROI and task was significant when focusing on the seven individual ROIs (F(2.04,38.83) = 5.29, p = 0.009).
source: When focusing on the seven individual ROIs, the interaction between ROI and task was significant (F(2.04,38.83) = 5.29, p = 0.009).
evidence: Direct statement of statistical test result.

claim: The difference in beta weights for number between the number and size task was highly significant from V3AB on.
source: Indeed the difference in beta weights between the number and size task was only minor or not significant in V1 and V2, more pronounced in V3, and highly significant from V3AB on (difference across tasks: V1: p = 0.025, Cohen's d = 0.64; V2: p = 0.13, Cohen's d = 0.37; V3: p = 0.001, Cohen's d = 0.91; V3AB p = 0.000001, Cohen's d = 1.44; V7: p = 0.000008, Cohen's d = 1.54; IPS12: p = 0.000001, Cohen's d = 1.56; IPS345: p = 0.000112, Cohen's d = 1.28).
evidence: Direct statement of statistical comparisons.

claim: Beta weights for density were positive both in early and in higher-level visual areas.
source: Density modulated early visual areas during the number task and both earlier and higher-level areas during the size task. The main effect of ROI was significant (F(1.41,26.72) = 4.05, p = 0.04), but additional post-hoc tests did not reveal any significant difference across the three large ROIs.
evidence: Statement about RSA results for density.

claim: Beta weights for density became significant in the parietal regions during the size task.
source: What we observed, however, was that beta weights for density obtained from RSA regression became significant in the parietal regions during the size task, suggesting that texture processing mechanisms may be automatically activated during the average size task.
evidence: Statement about RSA results for density during size task.

claim: Texture processing mechanisms may be automatically activated during the average size task.
source: What we observed, however, was that beta weights for density obtained from RSA regression became significant in the parietal regions during the size task, suggesting that texture processing mechanisms may be automatically activated during the average size task.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of density findings.

claim: The study used Representational Similarity Analysis (Kriegeskorte, 2008; Kriegeskorte and Kievit, 2013) to assess the effect of multiple quantitative dimensions on activity patterns simultaneously.
source: As a critical test of whether the representations of numerical and non-numerical features of the stimuli could be dissociated across the dorsal visual stream, we performed Representational Similarity Analysis (Kriegeskorte, 2008; Kriegeskorte and Kievit, 2013) which, unlike classification-based decoding, allows to assess the effect of multiple quantitative dimensions on activity patterns simultaneously.
evidence: Direct statement about analytical method with citations.

claim: The study applied multiple regression analysis to test in how far the fMRI pattern dissimilarity structure could be explained by multiple predictor matrices reflecting the stimuli's dissimilarity along several important quantitative dimensions.
source: We then applied multiple regression analysis to test in how far the fMRI pattern dissimilarity structure could be explained by multiple predictor matrices reflecting the stimuli's dissimilarity along several important quantitative dimensions: numerosity, average item size, total field area, total surface area and density (Figure 4B).
evidence: Direct statement about analytical approach with reference to Figure 4B.

claim: The design orthogonally manipulating numerosity, average item size and total field area ensured that numerosity was partly decorrelated from density and total surface area.
source: Of note, our design orthogonally manipulating numerosity, average item size and total field area ensured that numerosity was also partly decorrelated from density and total surface area (as shown by the correlation values in the Predictor Correlation matrix, Figure 4B), yet not completely (correlation between number and density predictors = 0.43; between number and total surface area predictors = 0.33).
evidence: Direct statement about stimulus design with reference to Figure 4B.

claim: Variance inflation factors (VIF) for each predictor remained reasonably low.
source: An estimation of variance inflation factors (VIF) for each predictor in our case revealed that these remained reasonably low (corresponding to 1.4874, 1.1957, 1.2048, 1.3238 and 1.4591 for number, average item size, total field area, total surface area and density, respectively).
evidence: Direct statement about statistical property of the regression model.

claim: The study used an equivalent number of most activated voxels in each region to train and test multivariate classifiers.
source: Within each region, we used an equivalent number of most activated voxels (in the orthogonal contrast 'all sample stimuli > baseline') to train and test multivariate classifiers to discriminate between numerosities for each task
evidence: Direct statement about voxel selection procedure.

claim: The included voxels mainly highlight the foveal portion of the different ROIs, in line with the central presentation of the dot arrays.
source: Figure 3B shows the across-subject overlap map for the included voxels which mainly highlight the foveal portion of the different ROIs, in line with the central presentation of the dot arrays.
evidence: Statement about voxel selection with reference to Figure 3B.

claim: The classification accuracy in the early visual areas remained nearly constant (62%) and was not significantly modulated by task (p = 0.5).
source: On the other hand, the classification accuracy in the early visual areas remained nearly constant (62%) and was not significantly modulated by task (p = 0.5).
evidence: Direct statement of classification results with statistical test.

claim: The change in classification accuracy across tasks was highly significant both for the intermediate and higher areas.
source: The change in classification accuracy across tasks was highly significant both for the intermediate and higher areas, (p = 0.001, Cohen's d = 0.88 and p = 0.00001, Cohen's d = 0.98).
evidence: Direct statement of statistical comparison.

claim: The classification accuracy increase in intermediate and higher areas with respect to early areas was very close to or clearly significant during the number task.
source: Post-hoc tests showed that the classification accuracy increase in intermediate and higher areas with respect to early areas was very close to or clearly significant (p = 0.075, Cohen's d = 0.52, and p = 0.028, Cohen's d = 0.57 respectively).
evidence: Direct statement of statistical comparison.

claim: During the size task, the classification accuracy in the intermediate and higher regions dropped down to 61% and 60% respectively, yet remaining highly significantly above chance in both cases.
source: During the size task, the classification accuracy in the intermediate and higher regions dropped down to 61% and 60% respectively (yet remaining highly significantly above chance in both cases, see p-values in Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Direct statement of classification results.

claim: The significant interaction between ROI and task was confirmed when testing the seven individual regions (F(4.10,77.97) = 7.17, p = 0.00005).
source: The significant interaction between ROI and task was confirmed when testing the seven individual regions (F(4.10,77.97) = 7.17, p = 0.00005).
evidence: Direct statement of statistical test result.

claim: The classification accuracy in individual regions significantly changed across tasks only from V3AB on.
source: Accordingly, the post-hoc tests indicated that the classification accuracy in individual regions significantly changed across tasks only from V3AB on (V1: p = 0.28, Cohen's d = 0.24; V2: p = 0.83, Cohen's d = 0.05; V3: p = 0.55, Cohen's d = 0.14; V3AB p = 0.0002, Cohen's d = 0.98; V7: p = 0.00003, Cohen's d = 1.20; IPS12: p = 0.00001, Cohen's d = 1.03; IPS345: p = 0.00005, Cohen's d = 1.26).
evidence: Direct statement of statistical comparisons.

claim: For the number task, the classification accuracy progressively increased from the early visual areas (slightly above 60%) to intermediate and higher level regions where it reached almost 70% correct.
source: For the number task, the classification accuracy progressively increased from the early visual areas (slightly above 60%) to intermediate and higher level regions where it reached almost 70% correct.
evidence: Direct statement of classification results.

claim: During the number task, the decoding accuracies progressively increased across the visual hierarchy and varied from slightly above 60% in the primary visual areas up to almost 70% in the intermediate and higher ROIs.
source: Although the post-hoc tests did not show significant differences in classification accuracies across individual ROIs, for the number task the decoding accuracies progressively increased across the visual hierarchy and varied from slightly above 60% in the primary visual areas (V1 = 62%, V2 = 62%, V3 = 61%) up to almost 70% in the intermediate and higher ROIs (V3AB = 64%, V7 = 65%; IPS12 = 67%, IPS345 = 67%).
evidence: Direct statement of classification results.

claim: During the size task, decoding accuracies were much reduced in intermediate and higher regions, while they remained almost unchanged in the primary visual areas.
source: During the size task, decoding accuracies were much reduced in intermediate and higher regions (V3AB = 58%, V7 = 58%; IPS12 = 59%, IPS345 = 58%, yet still significantly above chance in all ROIs, see p-values in Supplementary file 1), while they remained almost unchanged in the primary visual areas (V1 = 61%, V2 = 62%, V3 = 60%).
evidence: Direct statement of classification results.

claim: Activity patterns in V1, V2 and V3 were explained equally well by total field area and better than intermediate and higher regions, starting from V3AB on.
source: Indeed, activity patterns in V1, V2 and V3 were explained equally well by total field area and better than intermediate and higher regions, starting from V3AB on (all p < 0.01 at least).
evidence: Direct statement of statistical comparisons.

claim: Beta values for total surface area in the early visual areas were significantly higher than those estimated for the intermediate and higher-level ROIs, independent of the task.
source: The significant main effect of ROI (F(1.45,27.63) = 16.61, p = 0.000078) and the following post-hoc tests showed that beta values for this dimension in the early visual areas were significantly higher than those estimated for the intermediate (p = 0.000475, Cohen's d = 0.76) and higher-level (p = 0.000943, Cohen's d = 1.30) ROIs, independent of the task.
evidence: Direct statement of statistical test results.

claim: Beta weights for total surface area were comparable in V1, V2 and V3 and significantly higher than those of the others ROIs starting from V3AB/V7 on.
source: Beta weights for total surface area were comparable in V1, V2 and V3 (no significant difference across these ROIs) and significantly higher than those of the others ROIs starting from V3AB/V7 on (significant main effect of ROI: F(3.13,59.42) = 13.27, p = 0.000001, comparisons across regions: all p < 0.01 at least).
evidence: Direct statement of statistical test results.

claim: The main effect of ROI was significant for density (F(1.41,26.72) = 4.05, p = 0.04).
source: Density modulated early visual areas during the number task and both earlier and higher-level areas during the size task. The main effect of ROI was significant (F(1.41,26.72) = 4.05, p = 0.04), but additional post-hoc tests did not reveal any significant difference across the three large ROIs.
evidence: Direct statement of statistical test result.

claim: At the level of individual regions, the main effect of ROI was significant for density (F(2.55,48.55) = 4.15, p = 0.01).
source: Also at the level of individual regions the main effect of ROI was significant (F(2.55,48.55) = 4.15, p = 0.01) and the strongest difference across ROIs emerged when comparing the lowest beta weights estimated in V3AB with those obtained in V1 (p = 0.003, Cohen's d = 1.13) and V7, IPS12 and IPS345 (p = 0.03, Cohen's d = 0.20, p = 0.01, Cohen's d = 0.53, p = 0.002, Cohen's d = 0.64).
evidence: Direct statement of statistical test results.

claim: The model including only the orthogonal predictors (number, average item size and total field area) yielded results rather similar to the ones obtained with the full model.
source: Overall the results obtained with only the orthogonal predictors (i.e. number, average item size and total field area; see Figure 5—figure supplement 1) are rather similar to the ones obtained with the full model.
evidence: Statement about supplementary analysis with reference to figure supplement.

claim: In the model with only orthogonal predictors, the most important difference with respect to the full model appears to be a somewhat higher contribution of the number predictor, especially pronounced in early visual regions.
source: The most important difference with respect to the full model appears to be a somewhat higher contribution of the number predictor, especially pronounced in early visual regions.
evidence: Statement about difference between models.

claim: Results obtained from the model including only non-numerical dimensions were also similar to the full model.
source: Results obtained from the model including only non-numerical dimensions were also similar to the full model (see Figure 5—figure supplement 2 and p-values in Supplementary file 6).
evidence: Statement about supplementary analysis with reference to figure supplement.

claim: Only the most complete model including both numerical and non-numerical dimensions allows us to dissolve the ambiguity about whether effects observed for one given predictor are truly driven by that predictor.
source: Only the most complete model including both numerical and non-numerical dimensions allows us to dissolve this ambiguity.
evidence: Statement about the advantage of the full model.

claim: The study used linear support vector machines (SVM) with regularization parameter C = 1 for pattern classification analysis.
source: Pattern classification analysis was performed in scikit-learn (Pedregosa et al., 2011) using beta estimates after subtracting the voxel-wise mean across conditions by applying linear support vector machines (SVM) with regularization parameter C = 1.
evidence: Direct statement about classification method with citation.

claim: Classification analysis was performed leaving patterns of one run out at each loop of the 6-fold cross-validation cycle.
source: Classification analysis was performed leaving patterns of one run out at each loop of the 6-fold cross-validation cycle.
evidence: Direct statement about cross-validation procedure.

claim: Pairwise classification was performed for all pairs of numerosities collapsing across the size and total field area dimensions, but keeping patterns separated by task.
source: Pairwise classification was performed for all pairs of numerosities collapsing across the size and total field area dimensions, but keeping patterns separated by task.
evidence: Direct statement about classification procedure.

claim: The study used CoSMoMVPA Toolbox (Oosterhof et al., 2016) to create neural representational dissimilarity matrices.
source: Neural representational dissimilarity matrices (neural RDMs) for each task and ROI were created by computing the correlation distance (1 – the Pearson correlation across voxels) between activity patterns associated with all possible pairs of conditions using CoSMoMVPA Toolbox (Oosterhof et al., 2016).
evidence: Direct statement about analysis tool with citation.

claim: In the multiple regression analysis, all distance matrices were z-transformed before estimating the regression coefficients.
source: In the multiple regression analysis all distance matrices were z-transformed before estimating the regression coefficients.
evidence: Direct statement about preprocessing step.

claim: Participants performed six runs of approximately 7 min and 44 s during the scanning session.
source: Within the scanning session participants performed six runs of ~7 min and 44 s.
evidence: Direct statement about experimental procedure.

claim: Each run included four blocks where the two tasks alternated.
source: Each run included four blocks where the two tasks alternated.
evidence: Direct statement about experimental design.

claim: The type of task with which the run started was balanced across runs and participants.
source: The type of task with which the run started was balanced across runs and participants.
evidence: Direct statement about counterbalancing.

claim: The hands assigned to either the 'smaller' or 'larger' response were inverted in the middle of the scanning session and counterbalanced across subjects.
source: The hands assigned to either the 'smaller' or 'larger' response were inverted in the middle of the scanning session, that is after the third run, and counterbalanced across subjects.
evidence: Direct statement about counterbalancing procedure.

claim: Match stimuli were designed to be approximately 2 JNDs larger or smaller than the previously presented sample stimulus on the attended dimension.
source: Match stimuli were designed to be ~2 JNDs larger or smaller than the previously presented sample stimulus on the attended dimension, based on each participant's Weber fraction as measured in a behavioral test prior to the fMRI scanning, while the unattended dimension was the same as the previous sample stimulus.
evidence: Direct statement about stimulus design.

claim: Twenty trials were presented in each block: one trial for each one of the 18 sample stimulus conditions and two match trials.
source: Twenty trials were presented in each block: one trial for each one of the 18 sample stimulus conditions (3 numerosity x 3 sizes x two total field areas) and two match trials.
evidence: Direct statement about experimental design.

claim: Participants performed a behavioral test prior to the fMRI scanning to measure their numerical and average size acuity.
source: To measure their numerical and average size acuity, participants performed a behavioral test prior to the fMRI scanning.
evidence: Direct statement about experimental procedure.

claim: For each task, participants performed a total of 432 comparisons in the behavioral test.
source: For each task participants performed a total of 432 comparisons (6 numerosities x six average item sizes x two total field areas x two presentation order x three sessions).
evidence: Direct statement about behavioral test design.

claim: The JND was computed by fitting a cumulative Gaussian function using Psignifit toolbox (Schütt et al., 2016).
source: To quantify participants' precision in number and size judgments, we computed the JND for each task. The percentage of test trials with 'greater than reference' responses was plotted against the log-transformed difference between test and reference and fitted with a cumulative Gaussian function using Psignifit toolbox (Schütt et al., 2016).
evidence: Direct statement about analysis method with citation.

claim: Stimuli and paradigms were generated and presented under Matlab 9.0 using PsychToolbox routines (Brainard, 1997).
source: Stimuli and paradigms were generated and presented under Matlab 9.0 using PsychToolbox routines (Brainard, 1997).
evidence: Direct statement about software used with citation.

claim: EPI images were motion-corrected and co-registered to the first single band reference image using SPM12.
source: EPI images were motion-corrected and co-registered to the first single band reference image using statistical parametric mapping software (SPM12, https://www.fil.ion.ucl.ac.uk/spm/software/spm12/).
evidence: Direct statement about preprocessing step.

claim: Distortion correction was applied to all EPI images using topup and apply_topup in FSL.
source: The single-band reference images of the two initial volumes acquired with opposite phase encode directions served to estimate a set of field coefficients using topup in FSL (https://fsl.fmrib.ox.ac.uk/fsl/fslwiki/FSL), which was subsequently used to apply distortion correction (apply_topup) to all EPI images.
evidence: Direct statement about preprocessing step.

claim: Cortical surface reconstruction and boundary based registration were performed in Freesurfer.
source: Cortical surface reconstruction and boundary based registration of single band reference images to each subject's cortical surface, as well as a minimal amount of surface constrained smoothing (FWHM = 1.5 mm) for noise reduction were performed in Freesurfer (https://surfer.nmr.mgh.harvard.edu/).
evidence: Direct statement about preprocessing step.

claim: A minimal amount of surface constrained smoothing (FWHM = 1.5 mm) for noise reduction was performed in Freesurfer.
source: Cortical surface reconstruction and boundary based registration of single band reference images to each subject's cortical surface, as well as a minimal amount of surface constrained smoothing (FWHM = 1.5 mm) for noise reduction were performed in Freesurfer (https://surfer.nmr.mgh.harvard.edu/).
evidence: Direct statement about preprocessing step.

claim: The preprocessed EPI images were entered into a general linear model separately modeling the effects of the 36 sample conditions.
source: The preprocessed EPI images (in subjects' native space) were entered into a general linear model separately modeling the effects of the 36 sample conditions (3 numerosities x three average item sizes x two total field areas x two tasks, within each run the two repetitions for each condition were pooled together), the match stimulus separately for left and right hand and the written instructions at the beginning of the block as stick functions (using the default of 0 duration for events) convolved with the standard hemodynamic response function.
evidence: Direct statement about GLM design.

claim: The six motion parameters were included in the GLM as covariate of no interest.
source: The six motion parameters were included in the GLM as covariate of no interest.
evidence: Direct statement about GLM design.

claim: An AR(1) model was used to account for serial auto-correlation.
source: An AR(1) model was used to account for serial auto-correlation and low-frequency signal drifts were removed by a high-pass filter with a cutoff of 192 s.
evidence: Direct statement about GLM design.

claim: Low-frequency signal drifts were removed by a high-pass filter with a cutoff of 192 s.
source: An AR(1) model was used to account for serial auto-correlation and low-frequency signal drifts were removed by a high-pass filter with a cutoff of 192 s.
evidence: Direct statement about GLM design.

claim: Contrast images were projected onto the surface with Freesurfer, aligned to fsaverage and smoothed with a 3 mm fwhm Gaussian kernel.
source: After creating the contrasts in each single subject's volume space, the contrast images were projected onto the surface with Freesurfer, aligned to fsaverage and smoothed with a 3 mm fwhm Gaussian kernel.
evidence: Direct statement about preprocessing for group analysis.

claim: The second-level group analysis was performed in the surface space.
source: The second-level group analysis was then performed in the surface space.
evidence: Direct statement about group analysis.

claim: ROIs for V1 to IPS5 were created on the Freesurfer surface and projected back into each subject's volume space.
source: ROIs for V1 to IPS5 were created on the Freesurfer surface and projected back into each subject's volume space.
evidence: Direct statement about ROI definition procedure.

claim: For each ROI, the left and right hemisphere were merged.
source: For each ROI we merged the left and right hemisphere.
evidence: Direct statement about ROI definition.

claim: Within each bilateral region, 800 voxels that responded most strongly to the orthogonal contrast 'all sample stimuli > baseline' were selected for pattern recognition analysis.
source: Within each one of these bilateral regions we selected on a subject-by-subject basis an equal number of 800 voxels that responded most strongly to the orthogonal contrast 'all sample stimuli > baseline' for pattern recognition analysis.
evidence: Direct statement about voxel selection procedure.

claim: An overlap map was created to evaluate the degree of spatial consistency of the selected voxels across subjects.
source: To evaluate the degree of spatial consistency of the selected voxels across subjects we created an overlap map with Freesurfer (Figure 3B): single subjects' ROIs were aligned to fsaverage and the number of subjects for which a given location was included in their specific ROI was represented by a heat map (with yellow color meaning that a given location was selected in all subjects).
evidence: Direct statement about overlap map creation with reference to Figure 3B.

claim: Beta estimates were obtained after subtracting the voxel-wise mean across conditions.
source: Pattern classification analysis was performed in scikit-learn (Pedregosa et al., 2011) using beta estimates after subtracting the voxel-wise mean across conditions by applying linear support vector machines (SVM) with regularization parameter C = 1.
evidence: Direct statement about preprocessing for classification.

claim: Classifiers were trained on five betas per condition and tested with the left-out beta images.
source: This implies that classifiers were trained on five betas per condition and tested with the left-out beta images (one per condition).
evidence: Direct statement about cross-validation procedure.

claim: Classification accuracy was averaged across all pairs of numerosities for each task.
source: Classification accuracy was then averaged across all pairs of numerosities for each task.
evidence: Direct statement about averaging procedure.

claim: A one-sample t-test against the theoretical chance level of 50% was performed to evaluate significance of discrimination.
source: A one-sample t-test against the theoretical chance level of 50% was performed to evaluate significance of discrimination.
evidence: Direct statement about statistical test.

claim: Repeated measures ANOVAs were performed on classification accuracies with ROI and task as factors.
source: Repeated measures ANOVAs where then performed on classification accuracies with ROI and task as factors.
evidence: Direct statement about statistical analysis.

claim: For representational similarity analysis, the GLM was performed concatenating the runs and obtaining one single beta per condition, task and subject.
source: For representational similarity analysis (Kriegeskorte, 2008; Kriegeskorte and Kievit, 2013) the GLM was performed concatenating the runs and obtaining one single beta per condition, task and subject.
evidence: Direct statement about GLM for RSA with citations.

claim: Voxel-wise scaling was applied by subtracting the mean across conditions for RSA.
source: Comparable to the procedure of the pattern classification analysis, voxel-wise scaling was applied by subtracting the mean across conditions.
evidence: Direct statement about preprocessing for RSA.

claim: The obtained beta weights for each dimension and ROI were tested with one-sample t-tests against zero across subjects.
source: The obtained beta weights for each dimension and ROI were tested with one-sample t-tests against zero across subjects.
evidence: Direct statement about statistical test.

claim: The effects of ROI, dimension and task were analyzed with repeated measures ANOVAs.
source: The effects of ROI, dimension and task were analyzed with repeated measures ANOVAs.
evidence: Direct statement about statistical analysis.
